title: THEY BOTH LOVE JESUS. THEY BOTH BELIEVE THE BIBLE. SO WHY ARE THEY CALLING EACH OTHER UNFAITHFUL?
paragraphs: THEY BOTH LOVE JESUS. THEY BOTH BELIEVE THE BIBLE. SO WHY ARE THEY CALLING EACH OTHER UNFAITHFUL?

The painful debate over women serving as elders, the Greek words we cannot afford to ignore, and the dangerous moment when defending Scripture becomes an excuse to wound the very people Christ died to redeem.
She had served the church for twenty-three years.

She had prayed beside hospital beds. Taught children about Jesus. Comforted grieving mothers. Opened her home to struggling families. Shared the Gospel with people who had never stepped inside a church.
She knew Scripture. She loved Christ. Her life bore the unmistakable evidence of someone who had been walking with God through seasons nobody else knew about.
Then someone suggested she might be qualified to serve as an elder.
And suddenly, the conversations changed.
One person said, “God has clearly gifted her.”
Another responded, “But Scripture forbids it.”
Someone else whispered, “If you support women elders, you don't really believe the Bible.”
And before long, a woman who had spent decades serving Jesus found herself standing in the middle of a theological battlefield.
Not because she had denied the resurrection.
Not because she had rejected salvation by grace.
Not because she had abandoned the Gospel.
But because Christians who confessed the same Savior disagreed about how certain passages of Scripture should be understood.
Now imagine another believer.
A father. A faithful husband. A man who studies his Bible every morning before work. He sincerely believes God has reserved the governing office of elder for qualified men.
He doesn't hate women. He isn't trying to silence their testimonies. He believes women are equally created in God's image, equally redeemed by Christ, equally gifted by the Holy Spirit.
But he reads 1 Timothy 2 and 3 and believes obedience requires him to uphold a distinction between men and women in church leadership.
Then someone tells him, “Your position is hateful. You're standing against Jesus.”
And now he, too, is wounded.
Two believers.
Two consciences.
One Bible.
One Lord.
And a question that reaches much deeper than church leadership:
Can Christians disagree about whether women should serve as elders without questioning each other's faith?
Yes.
But that answer comes with a responsibility that neither side should escape.
We must take Scripture seriously enough to examine our interpretations, and we must take the Gospel seriously enough not to pronounce spiritual judgment where Christ has not authorized us to do so.
Because there is something profoundly troubling about a church that knows how to defend its position but has forgotten how to love its people.
And before anyone uses that sentence to dismiss doctrinal disagreement, hear this carefully.
Love does not make truth optional.
And truth does not make love disposable.
Jesus commands both.
The question is whether we are willing to obey Him when doing so costs us the satisfaction of winning an argument.
There is a reason this debate becomes so personal.
For some women, the question is not merely about a title. It touches years of feeling overlooked, dismissed, or treated as spiritually less capable.
For some men and women who hold the traditional position, the question is not about protecting privilege. It is about remaining faithful to what they sincerely believe God has commanded.
For others, the issue raises painful memories of church leaders who used biblical language to justify control, humiliation, or abuse.
And still others fear that cultural pressure is gradually persuading churches to abandon difficult biblical teachings.
These concerns are not identical.
They do not all lead to the same conclusions.
But they remind us that behind theological arguments are human beings carrying histories, convictions, fears, and wounds.
And Jesus sees every one of them.
So we cannot settle this debate by saying, “Everyone has their own truth.”
Christians do not have the freedom to manufacture truth according to preference.
Jesus prayed to the Father:
“Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.” — John 17:17, KJV
The Greek text says:
ἁγίασον αὐτοὺς ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ· ὁ λόγος ὁ σὸς ἀλήθειά ἐστιν.
Hagiason autous en tē alētheia; ho logos ho sos alētheia estin.
“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.”
That is not a call to surrender biblical conviction.
It is a call to submit our convictions to God's Word, even when Scripture challenges our assumptions.
And that submission begins with a difficult admission.
Sincere Christians can agree that Scripture is authoritative while disagreeing about how particular passages should be interpreted and applied.
That does not make every interpretation equally correct.
It means we must distinguish the authority of God's Word from our own understanding of it.
Those are not always the same thing.
Consider the passage at the center of the debate.
In 1 Timothy 2:12, Paul writes:
The Greek reads:
διδάσκειν δὲ γυναικὶ οὐκ ἐπιτρέπω οὐδὲ αὐθεντεῖν ἀνδρός, ἀλλ᾽ εἶναι ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ.
Didaskein de gynaiki ouk epitrepō oude authentein andros, all' einai en hēsychia.
A fairly direct rendering is:
“I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but to be in quietness.”
Now the difficulty begins.
The Greek verb αὐθεντεῖν (authentein) is unusually rare in surviving Greek literature, and scholars debate its precise nuance in this passage.
Some understand it as exercising authority in a relatively neutral sense.
Others argue that the context or usage suggests a more negative kind of authority, such as domineering or improperly assuming control.
The word itself does not settle the entire argument.
Neither does the English expression “usurp authority” in the King James Version settle the Greek meaning beyond dispute.
And ἡσυχία (hēsychia), commonly translated “quietness” or “silence,” can describe a quiet, peaceable disposition rather than necessarily absolute speechlessness in every setting.
That matters because Paul elsewhere acknowledges women praying and prophesying in 1 Corinthians 11:5.
We must read Scripture in conversation with Scripture.

Christians who hold the complementarian position generally understand 1 Timothy 2:12, especially in light of Paul's appeal to Adam and Eve in the following verses, as establishing a continuing restriction on women exercising the authoritative teaching and governing function associated with elders.

They also point to 1 Timothy 3:1–7 and Titus 1:5–9, where qualifications for overseers and elders include male-oriented descriptions, including the expression commonly translated “husband of one wife.”
They believe this pattern reflects God's ordering of the church rather than the spiritual inferiority of women.
That is a serious argument.
It deserves careful engagement.
It should not be dismissed as hatred simply because someone disagrees with it.
But Christians who hold the egalitarian position also bring biblical arguments that deserve honest consideration.
They point to women such as Priscilla, who participated with Aquila in explaining God's way more accurately to Apollos in Acts 18:26.
They point to Phoebe, whom Paul identifies in Romans 16:1 as a διάκονον (diakonon) of the church at Cenchreae.
The Greek term can refer to a servant, minister, or deacon, depending on context. Christians disagree about whether Phoebe held a formally recognized office.
They point to Junia in Romans 16:7, whom Paul mentions alongside Andronicus.

The Greek phrase ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις (episēmoi en tois apostolois) is disputed. Some understand it to mean that they were outstanding among the apostles; others understand it to mean they were well known to the apostles.
Even accepting the former interpretation would not, by itself, establish that Junia held the later church office of elder.
They also point to Galatians 3:28:
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
The Greek concludes:
πάντες γὰρ ὑμεῖς εἷς ἐστε ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
Pantes gar hymeis heis este en Christō Iēsou.
“For you are all one in Christ Jesus.”

Egalitarian interpreters argue that the New Testament's witness to spiritual gifting, mutual participation, and unity in Christ supports women serving in all offices, including eldership, when properly qualified.

Complementarian interpreters respond that equality in Christ does not necessarily eliminate every distinction in church responsibilities, and that Galatians 3:28 primarily addresses equal standing in Christ rather than qualifications for ecclesiastical office.
Both sides must reckon with the full biblical evidence.
Neither side should pretend the other has no passages to explain.
And neither side should turn a contested interpretation into an automatic verdict on someone's salvation.
Here is where the conversation becomes painfully revealing.
A Christian may be wrong about women elders without being wrong about who Jesus Christ is.
That sentence does not make the question insignificant.
Church leadership matters. Sound doctrine matters. Obedience matters. The way a congregation orders its ministry matters.
A church cannot simply avoid making a decision about who may serve as elders.

But the question of whether someone has correctly interpreted an elder qualification is not identical to the question of whether that person has genuinely trusted in the crucified and risen Lord Jesus Christ.
Paul reminds the Corinthians of the Gospel he preached:
“Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.” — 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, KJV
This is the center of the Christian proclamation.
Jesus Christ, the Son of God, died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Salvation is found in Him.
We are not saved by possessing a flawless understanding of every disputed question in church governance.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” — Ephesians 2:8, KJV
This does not mean doctrine is unimportant or that genuine faith can be separated from the call to obey Christ.
It means that we must not add our preferred resolution of a disputed ecclesiastical question to the saving work of Jesus.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to repent.
Not necessarily of our position.
But of our pride.
Of the careless words we used.
Of the motives we assigned to people whose hearts we could not see.
Of the way we made fellow believers feel like enemies when they were trying, however imperfectly, to honor the same Lord.
Have you ever walked away from a theological discussion feeling strangely victorious and spiritually empty?
You proved your point.
You quoted the passage.
You exposed the weakness in someone's argument.
But somewhere along the way, you stopped seeing a brother or sister and started seeing an opponent to defeat.
And maybe the other person did the same to you.
That is not a small thing.
Paul warned:

“And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.” — 1 Corinthians 13:2, KJV
The word translated “charity” is ἀγάπη (agapē), love.
Not sentimental agreement.
Not indifference to holiness.
Not pretending that contradictory teachings can both be true in the same sense.
Love.
The kind of love that refuses to dehumanize someone even while firmly disagreeing.
The kind of love that can say, “I believe your interpretation is mistaken,” without saying, “Therefore, you cannot belong to Jesus.”
The kind of love that remembers the cross before reaching for another accusation.
And we must be equally clear about something else.
Not every disagreement is harmless.
Not every church practice is faithful.
Not every appeal to conscience excuses disobedience.
The New Testament commands believers to guard sound doctrine and correct serious error.
Paul's instructions about elders are not optional simply because modern Christians find them controversial.
The church must study, pray, interpret, and act.
But the seriousness of a disagreement does not automatically make it a test of saving faith.

There may be circumstances in which a person's broader attitude toward Scripture raises genuine concerns about their doctrine. Yet those concerns must be evaluated fairly, rather than assumed merely because someone reaches a different conclusion about women elders.
A believer who rejects biblical authority outright is making a different claim from a believer who submits to biblical authority but understands a passage differently.
We should not confuse those two situations.
And this is not merely a lesson for those who disagree about eldership.
It is a mirror for all of us.
Because the human heart has an astonishing ability to disguise arrogance as discernment.
Sometimes we call it defending truth when we are actually defending our ego.
Sometimes we call it protecting unity when we are actually avoiding uncomfortable Scripture.
Sometimes we call it standing for women when we have stopped listening to women who hold traditional convictions.
Sometimes we call it standing for biblical authority when we have stopped listening to women who are faithfully studying and teaching God's Word within their understanding of Scripture.
Jesus does not ask us to choose between courage and humility.
He calls us to both.
And there is a scene in the Gospels that should unsettle every Christian who has ever used religious certainty to humiliate another person.
In John 8, religious leaders bring before Jesus a woman accused of adultery.
They place her in public view.
Her sin becomes the center of a confrontation.
But the passage reveals that they are also testing Jesus.

The scene is complicated by an important textual fact: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and its original place in the Gospel of John is disputed. It should therefore not carry the weight of establishing a doctrine by itself.
Even so, the familiar account vividly illustrates a danger that the undisputed teachings of Jesus also condemn: the use of another person's vulnerability as a weapon of religious self-righteousness.
Jesus does not celebrate sin.
He calls the woman away from it.
But He also exposes the accusers.
And the story leaves us with a haunting question.
What happens when people become more interested in condemning someone than in seeing that person restored?
Now apply that question carefully to the church.
A woman who believes she is called to serve as an elder is not thereby comparable to someone caught in adultery.
A man who believes eldership is reserved for qualified men is not thereby comparable to a malicious accuser.
The situations are not morally equivalent.
But the warning about the human heart remains relevant.
We can take a legitimate concern for righteousness and corrupt it through pride.
We can take a legitimate concern for inclusion and corrupt it through contempt.
We can speak about Jesus while behaving in ways that make His people afraid to be honest.
And that should grieve us.
Because the church is not supposed to be a place where every theological question becomes a public execution of someone's character.
It is supposed to be a people who belong to the One who was crucified for sinners.
Perhaps the most challenging biblical instruction for this debate is found in Ephesians 4:15:
“But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ.”
The Greek expression is:
ἀληθεύοντες δὲ ἐν ἀγάπῃ
Alētheuontes de en agapē.
Often rendered “speaking the truth in love,” the participle can convey the broader idea of being truthful or practicing truth in love.
Truth and love are not rival commitments.
They belong together in Christian maturity.
And the verse tells us where that maturity is supposed to lead.
Into Christ.
Not into a personality cult.
Not into theological tribalism.
Not into the satisfaction of having the final word.
Into Christ.
That changes the way we disagree.

It means a complementarian Christian can say, “I believe Scripture reserves eldership for qualified men, and I cannot in good conscience affirm women elders,” while still recognizing an egalitarian Christian as a brother or sister in Christ.

It means an egalitarian Christian can say, “I believe Scripture permits qualified women to serve as elders, and I believe the church should recognize those gifts,” while still recognizing a complementarian Christian as a brother or sister in Christ.
It means neither person must surrender conviction to practice Christian charity.
It also means churches should be honest about their convictions.
If a congregation believes the office is reserved for men, it should not mislead women about its governing beliefs.
If a congregation believes qualified women may serve, it should explain its biblical reasoning rather than treating every question as evidence of prejudice.
If members cannot agree on the practice, they may need to serve in different congregations.
That can be painful.
But separation over a significant church-order disagreement need not become a declaration that the other person is outside the family of God.
Sometimes Christian maturity means acknowledging that we cannot serve under the same governance arrangement while refusing to turn that difference into hatred.
And when a church has genuinely mistreated someone, reconciliation must involve more than asking the wounded person to be quiet for the sake of unity.
There must be truth.
Accountability.
Repentance.
And, where possible, restoration.
Biblical unity is not maintained by concealing injustice.
Nor is biblical truth protected by treating every disagreement as abuse.
We need more discernment than that.
We need more humility than that.
We need Jesus.
Because at the foot of the cross, every one of us arrives empty-handed.
The scholar and the struggling new believer.
The woman who has preached the Gospel faithfully for decades.
The man who has guarded his congregation's doctrine with tears and prayer.
The person who believes women should serve as elders.
The person who believes Scripture restricts that office to men.
None of us stands righteous before God because our theological arguments are impressive.
Our hope is Christ.
Our righteousness is not self-manufactured.
Our forgiveness was purchased at a price we could never pay.
And when we remember that, the tone of the conversation begins to change.
We still open our Bibles.
We still examine Greek words.
We still consider context, grammar, history, and the whole counsel of God.
We still make decisions.
We still correct error.
But we stop acting as though the blood of Jesus belongs exclusively to the people who agree with us about every disputed interpretation.
Imagine what could happen if two believers sat across from each other and began with a different question.
Not, “How can I prove you wrong?”
But, “Help me understand how you reached that conclusion from Scripture.”
Imagine a woman who had felt dismissed finally being heard without someone immediately assuming she was rebelling against God.
Imagine a man who held a traditional interpretation being heard without someone immediately assuming he despised women.
Imagine both opening their Bibles, acknowledging difficult passages, and admitting where their own arguments required careful explanation.
They might still disagree when the conversation ends.
But perhaps they would leave with something they had almost lost.
Respect.
A clearer understanding.
A willingness to pray for one another.
And the realization that Christian fellowship is bigger than the need to win every argument.
This is not theological weakness.
It is an expression of spiritual maturity.
James 1:19 says:
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
Some of us have become swift to post, swift to accuse, and slow to understand.
We can recognize an opponent's weakest sentence from a mile away, but we cannot recognize the pain in their voice.
We have learned how to defend the faith online while forgetting how to treat fellow believers with gentleness.
And perhaps the Holy Spirit is confronting something deeper than our position on women elders.
Perhaps He is confronting the condition of our hearts.
Are we willing to be corrected by Scripture?
Are we willing to acknowledge when we have misrepresented another Christian?
Are we willing to apologize without adding excuses?
Are we willing to defend truth without enjoying someone's humiliation?
Are we willing to admit that knowing the right answer does not automatically mean we have responded in the right spirit?
That last question may be the one we remember long after this article is forgotten.
Because there will come a day when our arguments will no longer be performed before an audience.
There will be no comment section to applaud us.
No followers to congratulate us.
No screenshots to prove we won.
We will stand before Jesus Christ.
And the Lord who commanded us to love one another will not be impressed by cruelty disguised as courage.
That should humble every side of this debate.
It certainly humbles me.
If you have been wounded by this argument, I pray you will not allow the sins of people to persuade you that Christ Himself has abandoned you.
If you have wounded someone while defending your interpretation, I pray you will have the courage to seek forgiveness.
If you are uncertain what Scripture teaches about women serving as elders, do not be ashamed to keep studying.
Read 1 Timothy 2–3.
Read Titus 1.
Read Acts 18.
Read Romans 16.
Read 1 Corinthians 11 and 14.
Read Galatians 3 in its context.
Consider the strongest biblical arguments on both sides rather than only the weakest statements of those you oppose.
Seek wise counsel from mature believers and faithful teachers.
And pray for a heart that would rather obey Jesus than protect its own reputation.
Because this discussion is not ultimately about making everyone comfortable.
It is about becoming faithful.
Faithful in our interpretation.
Faithful in our conduct.
Faithful in our treatment of one another.
Faithful to the Gospel that saved us.
And if this article has exposed something in your own heart, don't rush past it.
Maybe you have been carrying resentment toward someone who disagreed with you.
Maybe you have been afraid to ask sincere questions because you feared being labeled rebellious or unbiblical.
Maybe you have spoken about other believers in ways you would be ashamed to repeat in the presence of Jesus.
Or maybe you are exhausted by watching Christians wound each other over issues that deserve serious, prayerful examination.
What Scripture most shapes your conviction?
You do not have to explain your entire story publicly to be worthy of prayer.
Let the comments become a place where people reason from Scripture, share testimony, ask honest questions, and practice the respect we are talking about.
Not every disagreement needs another battlefield.
Sometimes it needs a table, an open Bible, and two people willing to listen.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, consider sending the article to them.
Not as a weapon.
Not as a subtle accusation.
But as an invitation to remember what unites Christians even when important disagreements remain.
There is another way you can help this ministry continue.
Behind every article, biblical resource, and discipleship effort is a desire to reach people who may never enter a church building but are still searching for hope, forgiveness, and truth.
Some are struggling believers.
Some are questioning their faith.
Some have been hurt by religious communities.
Some are hearing about the grace of Jesus Christ for the first time.
We want to keep bringing Scripture into those places.
We want those resources to remain accessible and to keep expanding the reach of this work.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That matters.
You never need to purchase God's favor.
Grace is not for sale.
These are simple reminders of our gratitude, not the reason anyone should give.
The greater purpose is to help keep the message of Jesus Christ moving beyond our immediate circle.
Because this ministry is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
The One who forgives sinners.
The One who restores the broken.
The One who confronts our pride without abandoning us to despair.
The One who calls His church to holiness and love.
The One whose grace is greater than our failures.
And this brings us back to the woman who had served faithfully for twenty-three years.
And to the man who sincerely believed the office of elder was reserved for qualified men.
What if neither had to become the villain in the other's story?
What if the church could evaluate their convictions seriously, uphold its understanding of Scripture faithfully, and still refuse to destroy their dignity?
What if our theological conversations became places where biblical truth was honored and the character of Christ was visible?

What if the next person who disagreed with us did not walk away thinking, “Those Christians know how to fight,” but instead thought, “They really do take their Bible seriously, and they really do love one another”?
That would not settle every doctrinal question.
But it would bear witness to something the world desperately needs to see.
Jesus prayed that His people would be one, and He connected their unity to the world's recognition that the Father had sent Him (John 17:20–23).
That unity is not permission to abandon truth.
It is a summons to live under the truth of Christ together.
We may disagree about who should serve as an elder.
We may have to make different decisions about church leadership.
We may even worship in different congregations because our convictions cannot be reconciled in practice.
But where we share genuine faith in the biblical Christ and His Gospel, we should be very careful before declaring that the other person does not belong to Him.
Jesus knows His own.
And we should tremble at the thought of treating someone He has redeemed as though they were beyond His grace merely because they disagree with our interpretation of a disputed passage.
So defend Scripture.
Study diligently.
Stand by conscience.
Correct error with patience.
Protect the vulnerable.
Repent when you have sinned.
And love the people Christ has commanded you to love.
Not because doctrine doesn't matter.
But because Jesus matters more than our pride.
And the church belongs to Him.
One day, the argument will fall silent—but the way we treated the people Jesus died for will still matter.
